analysis.one_liner: Gives internet users legal rights over their personal data and creates a federal agency to enforce them.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: after its introduction it was sent to four House committees, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Online Privacy Act would give people the right to see, correct, download, and delete the personal data companies hold about them, and to demand a human review of decisions made purely by algorithms. It would require companies to get permission before collecting, selling, or using personal data for targeted ads and profiles, ban manipulative consent screens, and outlaw collecting data in ways that discriminate by race, sex, or other protected traits. It would also create a new Digital Privacy Agency to enforce the rules, let state attorneys general and individuals sue violators, and make it a federal crime to post someone's personal information online to threaten or harass them.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday internet users gain enforceable rights over their personal information: access, correction, deletion, and portability of their data; consent before companies use their information for behavioral profiling or targeted advertising; notification of data breaches and data-sharing abuses; protection from discriminatory use of data in hiring, housing, credit, and advertising; and a criminal penalty for doxxing. Small businesses are largely exempted, so the burden falls on large data-intensive companies.

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals enforceable rights to access, correct, delete, and download the personal information companies hold about them, including what data was collected and which third parties received it [S2][S3].

Requires companies to get express consent before collecting, processing, or disclosing personal information, and to obtain separate consent before building behavioral profiles used to personalize content or ads [S2][S3].
Bars companies from using personal data to discriminate by protected class in employment, housing, credit, insurance, health care, and education opportunities [S2][S3].
Creates the Digital Privacy Agency to enforce the law, with penalties enforceable by the agency, state attorneys general, and private individuals, plus whistleblower protections [S2][S3].

Makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, to knowingly publish someone's personal information with intent to threaten, intimidate, harass, or incite violence against them [S3].
Protects encryption by forbidding companies from preventing users from encrypting their communications or from requiring them to hand over ways to decrypt them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large technology platforms, online advertising companies, and data brokers would bear the cost of compliance: consent systems, deletion and access mechanisms, data minimization, restrictions on selling data and targeted advertising, records of employee access, and a new regulator overseeing them. Some compliance costs could ultimately reach consumers through changes to ad-supported free services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big tech platforms and data brokers

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be costly and complex for covered companies, requiring new consent systems, access and deletion mechanisms, portability interfaces, and security programs; some of that cost could be passed to consumers through ads or prices [S3].
The bill creates an entirely new federal agency and moves privacy authority from the FCC, adding government spending and raising concerns about regulatory duplication and overreach [S2][S3].

Restrictions on behavioral personalization and the sale of data would curtail the targeted-advertising model that funds many free online services, and companies could deny service where no non-personalized version is feasible [S3].

Mandating data portability through public application programming interfaces could create security and engineering risks for platforms and favors companies positioned to exploit competitors' data [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give ordinary users substantial, enforceable control over their personal data and address real harms like discriminatory ad targeting, doxxing, and opaque algorithmic decisions. The costs fall mainly on large data-intensive companies, with small businesses exempted or given ramp-up time, which limits the economic downside. The most serious legitimate objections are the burden of a new federal agency, the engineering and security demands of mandated data portability, and disruption to ad-supported free services; the bill's breadth makes it genuinely ambitious rather than carefully incremental.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, none of which ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the Online Privacy Act of 2023 on April 19, 2023, joined by one cosponsor, Rep. Zoe Lofgren [S1][S3][S4].

The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Judiciary, House Administration, and Science, Space, and Technology Committees for consideration of provisions in their jurisdiction [S5].

No committee hearing, markup, or floor action followed; the bill's action history ends at the referral and it received no vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large tech platforms, online advertisers, and data brokers are better off: the restrictions on collecting, selling, and profiling personal data never took effect, and the status quo of largely self-regulated data collection continued.

for.name: Rep. Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Online Privacy Act of 2023, the most sweeping federal online privacy proposal of the Congress, giving individuals rights over their personal data and creating an enforcement agency.

for.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only other member of the House to sign on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary jurisdiction over privacy legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill after referral, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: House Judiciary, House Administration, and Science, Space, and Technology Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the provisions referred to them; the split referral across four committees required any movement to begin in multiple panels at once.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican supported or acted on the bill; it never reached a roll-call vote, so no voting breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill requires consent before disclosing personal data and restricts disclosing identifiers for advertising purposes, directly cutting into the market for tracking and selling people's data. Its business model depends on the practices the bill restricts, at a cost to users' privacy.

Platforms would face consent requirements, data minimization, deletion and portability duties, restrictions on profiling, and a dedicated regulator. They profit from collecting and personalizing data that the bill would put under user control.

Businesses under 200 employees with under $25 million revenue that do not sell data are exempt from most rights and duties, and may adopt larger companies' approved consent processes for free, sparing them compliance costs their bigger competitors would bear.
Mandated privacy-preserving computing, encryption protections, security policies, and breach notification would create demand for tools that help companies comply and protect users' data.
